title: How Narcolepsy Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain narcolepsy: a chronic sleep disorder marked by excessive daytime sleepiness (sleep attacks), with variants that add cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, disrupted nighttime sleep, and automatic behavior. They cover its history (Jean-Baptiste Édouard Gélineau, 1880, the wine merchant case), the Freudian explanations, REM-sleep links found in the 1960s, the 1990s discovery of hypocretin/orexin and its loss in type 1 narcolepsy, the HLA gene and autoimmune theory with strep infection, the 2009-2010 H1N1 swine flu vaccine Pandemrix linked to narcolepsy in Finland and the UK, diagnosis by polysomnography and multiple sleep latency test, treatments (stimulants, modafinil, SSRIs, hypocretin replacement research), and quality-of-life risks. The episode opens with personal anecdotes and closes with a listener mail segment about the Soul Train episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and personal anecdotes about narcolepsy
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter and share personal stories, including Chuck's great aunt Laura who had narcolepsy and fell asleep mid-sentence, and an unrelated family habit of after-dinner dozing. They note narcolepsy is more disruptive than people assume.

segments.title: Definition, history and early research
segments.summary: Narcolepsy is described as a chronic sleep disorder with excessive daytime sleepiness, first described in 1880 by French physician Jean-Baptiste Édouard Gélineau about a wine merchant who dozed hundreds of times a day. The hosts explain how total sleep over 24 hours can match normal levels, and discuss Freud's explanation, the 1960s finding of REM intrusion into wakefulness, and the 1990s focus on the hypothalamus.

segments.title: Narcolepsy types, cataplexy and the core symptoms
segments.summary: The hosts describe type 1 narcolepsy (with cataplexy) and type 2 (without), explain cataplexy as sudden loss of muscle control while conscious, often triggered by positive emotions, and list the symptoms: excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hallucinations, disrupted nighttime sleep, and possibly automatic behavior. Onset is usually in adolescence and cataplexy can improve with age.

segments.title: Sleep paralysis, hallucinations and disrupted night sleep
segments.summary: The hosts describe sleep paralysis during sleep onset and waking, hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucinations often including a sense of a presence, and disrupted nighttime sleep as the reverse of daytime sleepiness. They discuss the hypothalamus and hypocretin as the switch holding sleep and wakefulness apart.

segments.title: Hypocretin/orexin discovery and cause in the brain
segments.summary: Hypocretin, also called orexin, was isolated in the 1990s; it helps maintain wakefulness and boosts other neurochemicals. People with type 1 narcolepsy have far fewer hypocretin-producing neurons, roughly 100,000 to 200,000 neurons in the rear of the hypothalamus. Type 2 patients show no such decrease, and sleep state instability is thought to underlie the sleepiness.

segments.title: Genetics, autoimmunity, strep infection and H1N1 vaccine link
segments.summary: Narcolepsy is linked to a variant of the HLA gene and is thought to be an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks hypocretin-producing neurons, possibly triggered by strep infection. The hosts describe the Pandemrix H1N1 swine flu vaccine, which was linked to increased narcolepsy cases in Finland and the UK, with affected children carrying the HLA variant, and mention personalized medicine as a way to avoid this.

segments.title: Diagnosis, treatment, and quality of life
segments.summary: Diagnosis involves an overnight polysomnography and a multiple sleep latency test, with cerebrospinal fluid testing for hypocretin levels as an option. There is no cure, but treatments include stimulants like modafinil, SSRIs, and experimental hypocretin replacement. Narcolepsy is often underdiagnosed and co-occurs with depression. The hosts discuss accident risk, workplace accommodations under the Americans with Disabilities Act, and the suicide of Katie Clack, who developed narcolepsy after a vaccine.

segments.title: Listener mail: Soul Train feedback
segments.summary: Listener Julia, president of the Tybee MLK Human Rights Committee, praises the Soul Train episode and mentions the magazine Right On and the cultural significance of the show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and give the email address for feedback.
